fields.meta_title: IT Request Form Builder With Priority Routing | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build an IT request form that sets priority from impact and urgency, finds spare license seats and routes tickets to the right tech. Free to start.
fields.h1: Build an IT Request Form That Triages Every Ticket
fields.hero_description: Describe the requests your IT team handles and who answers each one. Emergent turns that into an IT request form with triage and a table of every ticket.
fields.features_heading: What the Form Asks, and What It Does Next
fields.features_subheading: A vague ticket means a round of follow-up questions. These pieces get the detail up front and pass each request on.
fields.feature_1:
Request type picked first

The first question asks whether the request is a fault or a new ask. Each answer opens its own follow-ups: an outage asks who is affected, and a software request names the app.
fields.feature_2:
Priority from impact and urgency

Ask for the number of people hit and whether work has stopped. The pair of answers sets priority on a fixed grid. One slow laptop never outranks a whole team that cannot work.
fields.feature_3:
License seats checked on request

Connect the license list IT already pays for. A software request looks for an unused seat first and assigns it once the manager approves, before anyone raises a purchase order.
fields.feature_4:
Routing by building or team

Send each ticket to the technician who covers that building or that department. The assignee gets a Slack message or an email with the details and any screenshots attached.
fields.feature_5:
Quotes before billable work

Managed IT providers mark which requests a client's contract covers. Anything outside it gets a quote at the hourly rate, and no work starts until the client approves the price.
fields.feature_6:
Your code, in your GitHub

Export the full IT request app to your own repository whenever the team wants it in-house. The ticket table goes with it, along with each status change and who made it.

fields.usecase_heading: Four IT Requests, Handled After Submit
fields.tab_content_1:
Eighteen stalled adjusters make it a P1

Larkspur Insurance runs claims from one shared system. When it stops loading, a supervisor files a request: 18 adjusters affected, work stopped. Those two answers set the ticket at P1 on the priority grid. The on-call technician, Ravi Menon, gets a Slack message with the error screenshot attached.
fields.tab_content_2:
A spare seat goes out before a new license is bought

Fernhill Studio pays for 25 seats of its design software. Nora Diaz, a junior designer, requests one for a client project. A check of the license table finds 2 seats unused since staff left in the spring. Once her manager approves, IT assigns one of those seats, and no new license is bought.
fields.tab_content_3:
Before the 10:00 lecture, Hale Hall's technician has the ticket

Ashford College assigns a technician to each teaching building. A lecturer reports that the projector in Hale Hall room 214 shows no signal, with her class starting at 10:00. The form reads the building and the start time, sends the ticket to Owen Price, who covers Hale Hall, and marks it to fix before class.
fields.tab_content_4:
Out-of-contract work waits for the client's yes

Kettle IT supports dental offices on monthly contracts that cover support but not new setups. Pine Street Dental asks for a laptop setup for a new hygienist. It is flagged as outside the contract, and the office manager, Carla Reyes, gets a quote for 2 hours at $120. Work waits until she approves the $240.

fields.howto_title: How to Create an IT Request Form
fields.howto_description: Most IT tickets are one of two kinds: something broke, or someone needs something new. Settle how each kind is handled before you write the prompt.
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Ask for what a technician needs
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Describe the form in a prompt
fields.howto_step_1_des: Pull last month's tickets and split them into broken things and new asks. ITIL calls the first incidents and the second service requests. Incidents need a priority and a fast response. Service requests, such as a new app, usually need an approver.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Settle two questions with the help desk: how many people are affected, and can they still work. Write down which priority each pair of answers produces and how fast a technician should respond at each level, before the form goes live.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Ask for the detail a technician needs to start without calling back: the device or app, the exact error, when it began, and a screenshot. Have the description field ask what the requester was trying to do, since that is where unclear tickets go wrong.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Tell Emergent the request types and who handles each one. Emergent builds the IT request form, the routing rules and a ticket table in a database you own. Change a rule later by describing the change in the same chat, and the app updates.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Connect the lists IT already keeps
fields.howto_step_5_des: Connect the license register and the list of which technician covers which building. The form reads both on each request. A spare seat turns up and a technician is picked without anyone checking a spreadsheet by hand first.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Decide what the requester sees after submitting: a ticket number and the name of whoever has it. Send updates by email or Slack whenever the status changes. People who can see progress stop filing the same problem twice under a new subject line.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 File one request of each type
fields.howto_step_7_des: Before launch, send a test ticket that should land at the top priority and another that needs approval. Check that each reaches the right person and that both show up in the table with a status history from the first minute.

plan.angle: The live top 10 is blank templates (BlockSurvey, PandaDoc, two Jotform pages, LiveAgent, pdfFiller), one university service portal (LSU) and a Spiceworks thread where an admin asks how to stop vague requests like 'need Power BI license' that start a round of questions. Google's AI Overview and image pack show the same field lists. No result shows what happens after a request is filed. This page answers the Spiceworks question with the fields that decide each request, then shows four request types handled after submit: a team-wide outage scored by impact and urgency and sent to the on-call tech, a software request filled from an unused license seat, a classroom fault routed to the technician for that building, and out-of-contract work at a managed IT provider held for the client's approval. The FAQ covers templates, PDF, Word and Excel versions, free options and hardware requests.
